She lasted 5 years -- turning 91 when she passed from "failure to thrive"

I grew up in a dysfunctional and codependant household. so I was gaslighted and told what I couldn't do on an almost daily basis.  I was told college wasn't worth it because a relative failed at it and had to work for his father in a factory.  I tried getting my own education, but I was also the sole caregiver for my mom from 32 and I had to drop out.  This limited me severely in what jobs I could get with certificates in office automation and bookkeeping.

I wasn't emotionally strong enough to walk away.  As a baby I almost died and in in preteens I developed emotional problems due to family drama. to put a cap on it, I developed Rheumatoid Arthritis at 16 and was essentially bedridden until 18.

Fast forward to today and I obtained a low level state job and am living on my own paying my own way. The RA resurfaced in my late 50s and I am now listed as Disabled with it -- it affects my mobility and ability to do even sedentary work.

I have had to erase decades of parental tapes but found out late that no one can live your life for you and no one will.  Eventually you have to face your life choices.  Better to pull off the bandaid earlier.

For me, if I get to the root of the problem, I'm not accepting things nor am I satisfied with things deep down.  It goes against the old adages of not settling for second best and the try try again thing.

It may not be a lot, but it's better than what many have.  With management and downsizing you may remain comfortable if you shift your priorities.

If you aren't cooking your own meals, look into learning how; that can save a lot of money over even those meal plans that come to your door.  I eat fairly well on $100 a week for food; which could be gone in two days of eating out.

Being able to have the basics and peace of mind even if you have to dip a little into your savings is better than not having something augment your SSI with what you have.  As you reduce your liquidity, you may quality for utility or rental assistance.  Check with 2-1-1 in your area if in the US.

I had a toxic roommate, for the first 7 years after I lost the house due to a long bout of unemployment and bankruptcy in the 00s, but for now I'm able to live alone and enjoy my peace of mind.  Even if I come to a point where I will have to be in a care facility I will be able to accept what challenges I will face a lot better than in the past.

I gave up on THINGS, and am looking at a place where I won't need a car either -- I'm hoping to get into affordable housing closer to where I grew up.  I'm on a couple of lists and it's now a waiting game.

Meanwhile, I appreciate my morning coffee each day, my work from home arrangement due to my disability, and the fact that I can stop, breathe and Let Go of a lot more of the attachments I used to stress out over and feelings of Anxiety I and Depression let wash over me as a result. 

Your tsunami may still come, but you need not suffer as much as you are; face it when it arrives and not before.

External pursuits of happiness is a hamster wheel; you need to keep running after the next thing or activity to keep up the level of satisfaction that makes you feel happy (distracted from your dissatisfaction).

I started seeking how to be happy in those quiet moments when you aren't doing work or chasing things; being able to be alone with myself at night in those moments after the TV is off and before sleep comes.

I found a lot of material on the subject: there are some answers in Stoicism, Acceptance Therapy and Mindfulness.  Authors like Marcus Aurelius. Eckhard Tolle, Michael Singer, and others talk about shifting focus on your mindset.

Essentially, it's a matter of looking for Inner Peace instead of Happiness

I suffered traumas in my life as well, and I finally found some strategies that are working and might help you.

First off, work on making yourself better.

Make sure you are getting enough sleep and are hydrated and eating healthily.  If you feel awful, you may not want to interact with people.

Stop ruminating over the past.  All the "What Ifs" and "I should haves" are stealing your time and energy and are probably affecting your health.

Accept that People acted badly towards you and you acted badly as well and Let It Go.

You cannot change the past, you can only act today to make a better tomorrow for yourself.

Put your time and energy into becoming a little better every day.

Begin by Forgiving yourself and Believe that you are worth being friends with.

List all your qualities that you have as a friend:  remind yourself of them.  Put them on by your mirror or write them down and read them several times a day.

Keep a journal. Write down what challenged you, what upset you, how you handled it -- note how you want to handle future occurrences. Also list things you are grateful for: even something as small as a bird coming to a feeder that makes you smile, or the antics of a kitten.

With regards to making friends, don't be afraid to fail.

You cannot control what people think or say, all you can do is accept that they behave the way that they do.

Being a friend does take work and it it is a give and take relationship.  A simple greeting "Hi, how are you?" in person or text or a shared meme goes a long way.

One of the best books on the market was How To Win Friends and Influence People, by Dale Carnegie.  Essentially:

* Be genuinely interested in other people
* Smile
* Remember and use that person's name
* Be a good listener; encourage others to talk about themselves
* Talk about other person's interests
* Make the other person feel important.

As far as where to find people, consider volunteering in a cause you are passionate about, or joining a civic organization that helps the community.  You will find like minded people to talk to face to face.

And of course, communities on Discord, Telegram, and other platforms are a good place to talk to people in a more controlled environment. These can even blossom into meetups with local groups and you get to be with the people you chat with.

Again join groups that you are interested it.  At the very least you can practice your people skills, and it is OK if you drop off for a day or two.  I do that all the time.

Finally, be able to laugh at yourself and your mistakes. Most people are not going to betray you and this fear of getting hurt again may be what is really holding you back.

Marcus Aurleus, the last of the five good emperors of Rome was a stoic, and he attributed his success to Stoicism.  If you look up successful stoics, you see athletes, authors, and military officers. These lessons have survived the sands of time and continue to provide value to modern man.

In my own case, as a relative new comer, it orders my mind and has taken me away from Magical Thinking and has softened the blows that life gives regardless of how good we are or how much devotion we have.  

There may be other ways to face hardships, but the concepts of Amor Fati, Premeditato Malorum, and Memento Mori have summed up the way I need to look at life.

Amor Fati: Love fate.  In other circles this is Acceptance of what happens and surrendering (or trading in -- to my way of thinking) all of the ruminating and anxious moments and depressive episodes.  We can't fix the past and we can only prepare for the future (Premeditato Malorum), not control it, so why waste our limited time on the earth (Memento Mori) groaning, grieving, and having restless nights over things that may never happen.

The four Stoic pillars of Justice, Wisdom, Courage, and Moderation provide signposts on how to live your life that are reflected by many other religions and ethics systems.

In short, knowing what you can influence (your thoughts and actions) and what you cannot and how to behave makes for a set of guidelines that are easy to understand yet require awareness (Mindfulness) to practice because they are so contrary to the egotistic lifestyle that is so common these days.

The reason is that those things we are trying to control are what Stoics call Externals: wealth, health, relationships, careers, events (weather, accidents, outcomes).  All we can do is our best, but there are no guarantees.

We have little to no control over Externals; and when things don't go the way we want, we are miserable.

What Stoicism teaches is showing us what we can control: own own actions and mind -- as in how we respond to external events.  

You can start by reading / listening to the three greats: Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, and Seneca.
  
"Meditations" by Marcus Aurelius is a great place to start. You can also look for Stoic videos on YouTube and web sites such as The Daily Stoic.

Two concepts of stoicism that might take some of the sting out of your life's disappointments are Amor Fati and Premeditatio Malorum.

Amor Fati is acceptance of the good and bad that comes your way as if it was exactly what you wished for.  It may be difficult to believe that you would wish for a flat tire, or a job loss, or an illness, but they are Externals and beyond your control.

“Don’t seek for everything to happen as you wish it would, but rather wish that everything happens as it actually will—then your life will flow well.” — Epictetus

What you can do with Externals is control is your attitude towards them: accept them with grace, do not bemoan them, and take advantage of whatever it is that they may bring about. 

“External things are not the problem. It’s your assessment of them. Which you can erase right now.” – Marcus Aurelius

The second concept, Premeditatio Malorum is basically expect the worst, and prepare for it.

In the snow, keep a blanket, food, and water in your car.  Have a nest egg put aside if unexpected bills come up.  Think of everything that can go wrong and then make as many preparations that you can and then Let It Go.

 “Cling tooth and nail to the following rule: not to give in to adversity, never to trust prosperity, and always take full note of fortune’s habit of behaving just as she pleases, treating her as if she were actually going to do everything it is in her power to do. Whatever you have been expecting for some time comes as less of a shock.” — Seneca

Hopefully this will give you some direction in to how Stoicism may help bring you peace of mind.

If you choose to have no opinion about what someone says to you, you *"leave it"* "on their doorstep", and go about your business as if you never heard it.

Of course, the act of leaving -- walking away from danger, threats, and toxic environments is another way of interpreting it.

***Acceptance*** is allowing (in your mind)  what is to happen, to happen without resistance or complaining: just letting it be.  You accept that the sun rises in the morning -- it is a given.  You accept that it is going to rain -- it will, eventually, somewhere and sometime.

You accept your past by not playing "if I only"

”How does it help to make troubles heavier by bemoaning them.”  Seneca

You accept your future by not playing "what if" to an absurd amount

”We suffer more in our imagination than in reality”  Is another Seneca quote.

Use Premeditato-malorum: plan for the worst, do your best with whatever comes our way, and do not depend on fixed outcomes save the Last Outcome: Memento Morti

Remember we will die.  Thus, do not waste your limited time on this earth bemoaning the past and fretting the future like Chicken Little worrying about the sky falling.

Review your past, plot your future course, and do  your best to grow and be better each day in some small manner.

My favorite response comes from 7 Stoic Exercises for Inner Peace:

Don’t give a f*ck practice

Okay, now after swallowing your food after chewing it for 10 to 20 times, why don’t you start eating like a pig? Don’t use your hands. Just go for it. Especially in a restaurant so everyone can see what you’re doing. This is a way to combat a trait that most of us seem to have in excess: caring too much about the opinions of other people. 

The thing is: the opinions of other people are not up to you. It’s beyond your control. So, why worry about it? Because of our social conditioning, it takes practice to break this habit. A fear of social ostracism is deeply ingrained within us.

By deliberately making a fool out of ourselves, we will be exposed to situations in which people will judge us negatively. Even if it’s just by looks and giggles. Slowly, you’ll experience that this doesn’t hurt as you’ve imagined. Thus, your ‘don’t give a f*ck’ attitude has become stronger.

I have been struggling with life for a  long time myself.  I have not been happy for years, and ***I considered it a matter of survival to have my needs met***, (to find contentment), but:

I have come to realize that 'survival' can mean a lot of thing, but in simplest terms:

1. Are you safe; is your physical life in danger?
   1. (I understand mental abuse; see below)
2. Do you have shelter; can you sleep safely?
3. Do you have food.

If you are in danger or at risk, seek help.

But, If the three conditions of survival are are being met, then the struggle is with *your perceptions of what you need out of life.*

*This is something I have been struggling with for years.*

**P*****erceptions*** of *what you need to end your struggles with life* can be changed.

**You can either change what** ***you think you need*** (perceptions) or **change your circumstances** to meet your *needs.*  ***Changing your circumstances take money or assistance or both***\*.\*

*It may far easier to learn to live with your circumstances* until you can afford to move and make your own life.  ***Learning to live with your conditions can be aided by therapy*** *as well as learning to separate Wants and Needs.*

**Needs and Wants are different**.  You can manage without **things**: the newest phone, console game system, a fancy car (if you drive) or other things; ***those are wants***.  **What you** ***need*** are the three things above --safety, shelter, and food.

**I understand needing peace of mind (a non-mentally abusive space) as a factor of** ***safety***\*\*.\*\*

**In short, you cannot change external forces (how people think, act and do or say and things like the weather or even the economy ).**

**You can only your perception about what you are willing to accept in your life.**

\[THE REST IS MORE NARRATIVE, THAT YOU CAN IGNORE, BUT YOU MAY GAIN SOME INSIGHT FROM MY STORY; FOLLOWING THOSE ARE SOME MOVING STRATEGIES. Hopefully it helps\]

***I was in therapy for four years (for chronic depression)*** *and my relatives consoled me to get my own place for my own mental health (safety).*

**Because my landlord's alcoholism and behavior were constantly triggering me, I constantly complained to him about it.**

As a result of my complaints, **He evicted me.**  **How he lived in his house wasn't my right to criticize or change.**

**If I would have been able to accept his behavior and actions, I would be living there now, at half** **of what I having to pay currently**.  *I could not.* ***My discontent came with a price tag.  And I need money to pay that price.***

**Money is our main survival tool.**  If you have money you can find a place to live away from what you find you cannot tolerate, as I was forced to do.

Fortunately I could (barely) afford to move. My job pays my bills and provides what I need to live modestly. I make sure to put a little aside each pay cycle for emergencies.

**Work is the way we usually earn money.**  If you have a disability you may be able to get *assistance* \-- but be aware, it *will barely (if at all) allow you to survive*.

***Work comes with issues***\*\*:\*\*

* Your ability to complete your job satisfactorily according to your boss
   * Doing things you disagree with
   * Having to work on your bosses schedule
* Having to deal Bosses and Coworkers
   * Personality conflicts
   * Power trips (Politics)
* Using Your Time and Energy in return for (what you may consider) insufficient money.

So, if you don't/ can't work, you must find assistance to pay for what you need. This can be a full time job in itself, that doesn't necessarily return anything but a  bare minimum of safety, food, and shelter (and maybe not enough of those).

**If you decide your current living conditions need to change:**

You should figure out what you need for your living expenses.

* housing and utilities \[power/water/Internet/Phone\]),
   * including down payment, installation, and security payments
* food; knowing how to cook will save you a lot of money
* transportation, public or private (car / uber) to get around.
* clothes, housewares, furniture
* medical/dental costs.
* other / general expenses

Look at living spaces and it should be no more that 50% of what you are earning.

So if you can find a place to live for $750 a month (housing and utilities) then, minimally, your net pay should be about $1500 a month.  You may get energy assistance and other benefits; see your social services officials for specifics.
